# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Critical reading of Varga and Holm's comment on the Halden pilot

**Bottom line:** Sections 1–4 are a valuable correction to the Halden working paper. They use the pilot's own microdata, quantify each problem, and are candid about subsets in the data note. The conclusion goes beyond that evidence. The authors' own best estimate is a *positive* per-hour gain of 10.8%, and they dismiss it using an untested novelty argument. They also treat the Varden trial selectively: they accept its negative counter result as "the most reliable finding" while ignoring its positive case-processing result, which closely matches their own corrected figure. "Most of the gain is artifact" is supported. "Entirely an artifact" is not.

## 1. Arithmetic

Most figures check out:

- **Table 2:** 95.1 / 0.800 gives +18.9%. Hours of 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859, and 98.4 / 0.859 gives +14.6%. Hours of 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861, and 95.4 / 0.861 gives +10.8%.
- **Hours fall:** 40.3 to 34.6 is −14.1%, so the reduction was overstated by about 6 points.
- **Real revenue:** 1.014 / 1.041 is about 0.974, or −2.6%.

**The hours decomposition does not add up.** Four days at about 8.0 hours plus 0.7 extra each gives about 34.8 hours. Adding 1.6 hours on the day off gives about 36.4 hours. The reported pilot average is 34.6. Matching 34.6 would require only about +0.25 extra hours per day, or almost no day-off work. Possible explanations include:

- one component is misstated;
- the components come from different subsets; or
- the 0.7 is relative to some other baseline.

This needs fixing. If the components are right and the total is wrong, actual hours fell even less and the per-hour gain shrinks further.

**The novelty extrapolation is slightly off.** The energy score fell from 0.61 to 0.29 SD between months 3 and 6, about −0.107 SD per month. A straight line from those two points reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." This is minor, but it is the kind of precision a methods comment should get right.

## 2. What the comment does well

- **Attrition.** If the microdata are right, the working paper misdescribed its withdrawals. Seven of the nine organisations left *after* the reduced schedule began, and six cited workload or output, not scheduling. This is a serious reporting discrepancy, and the Halden authors should answer it directly.
- **Output measure.** Comparing manager ratings with organisations' own records is exactly the right check. The direction is consistent: managers rated higher in 19 of 23 organisations, with a mean gap of 3.8 points.
- **Hours.** It replaces Halden's scheduled-hours denominator with logged hours. Varden made the same correction and found the same direction and a similar size of overstatement.
- **Revenue.** It is right to point out that the 1.4% was nominal. CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue, since sector producer prices would be better, but the point stands.
- **Sectoral claims.** Section 5 correctly notes that any output index above 80 registers as a per-hour gain when hours fall 20%.
- **Data note.** It honestly states that the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets.

## 3. Problems with the comment

### The abstract claims a correction that was never made
The abstract says the 10.8% comes from "correcting the first three" problems, which would include attrition. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. It still uses survivors only. Attrition is described but never quantified. There are no bounds, no intention-to-treat estimate, and no imputation for the nine organisations that withdrew. Attrition probably pushes the estimate down, but the comment does not show by how much.

### Table 2 mixes corrections with changes in sample
Each row of Table 2 uses a different sample: 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. The step changes therefore combine two things: the effect of each correction, and differences between the organisations in each subset. Reporting all four specifications on the same 17 organisations would isolate the corrections.

### There is no uncertainty anywhere
None of the corrected estimates has a confidence interval. With 17 organisations, the interval around 10.8% is likely wide. Without it, the reader cannot tell whether the data rule out zero, which is precisely what an "entirely an artifact" claim requires.

### "Record-based output" may be biased downward
Some of the submitted records are billable hours delivered. In a reduced-hours trial, that is closer to an input than an output: if people work fewer hours, billable hours fall almost by definition. Organisations measured this way would push the record-based index down mechanically. The comment should report how many of the 23 used billable hours and show results without them.

### The record gap may not be all manager bias
Managers may have rated broader output that a single recorded metric misses. The 19-of-23 pattern makes bias plausible, but some of the 3.8-point gap may reflect what each measure covers.

### Novelty is asserted, not tested
The comment's case for novelty rests on two points of a self-reported *energy* scale, extended in a straight line. That approach has several weaknesses:

- **Energy is not output.** Nothing shows that output per hour followed the energy decline.
- **Two points cannot establish a linear trend.** The scale could just as well be levelling off.
- **The direct test was available and not run.** The microdata contain *monthly* manager output indices, and for some organisations monthly records and time logs. Tracking output per hour month by month would test novelty directly.

"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is a rhetorical move, not evidence. Novelty is one hypothesis, and the comment leaves it untested.

### The comment ignores half of the Varden trial
The comment calls Varden's counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature." That result comes from 5 v 5 offices, with the few-cluster inference problems I noted earlier.

The same trial, with the same design, randomisation and record-based actual-hours measurement, found **+12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4) per actual hour in case-processing**:

- It comes from 7 v 7 offices, a somewhat larger stratum than the counter one.
- It ran for nine months, longer than Halden's six.
- It had a concurrent control group.
- It is very close to the comment's own corrected +10.8%.

Two independent sources, one randomised, now converge on a gain of about 10–13% per actual hour in backlog-type work. Treating one Varden stratum as decisive while ignoring the other is selective use of evidence.

### The meetings critique misdescribes Varden's analysis
- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known."** The calendar data were collected in month six of a nine-month trial, before the final results existed.
- **"Fitted to a subgroup."** The seven offices are *all* the treated case-processing offices, a pre-specified stratum, not a chosen subset.
- **Varden's actual claim.** Its authors already said the analysis was unregistered, that seven offices cannot establish a mechanism, and that they have registered a confirmatory test. The comment attacks a stronger claim than the one Varden made.

The meetings hypothesis also cuts against "artifact." If cutting meetings raises output per hour, the gain is *real*, just not caused by rest. It may also be achievable without cutting hours. That changes the policy question, but it is not measurement error.

### Inconsistent and overgeneralised conclusions
- **"Most" becomes "entirely."** The abstract says the four problems "account for most of the reported gain." The conclusion says gains are "entirely an artifact." Only "most" is supported.
- **One pilot becomes all schemes.** The conclusion extends from a single pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" in general.
- **It contradicts its own data note.** The note says the corrected estimates describe subsets, not the pilot as a whole, yet the conclusion generalises beyond even the pilot.

## 4. Where the three documents leave the evidence

| Question | Best current reading |
|---|---|
| Was Halden's 23.4% too high? | Yes, clearly. Manager ratings, scheduled hours and survivor sampling all inflated it. |
| Is there a real per-hour gain in backlog-type work? | Probably about 10–13% over 6–9 months. Halden corrected (+10.8%, non-random subset, no CI) and Varden case-processing (+12.5%, randomised) agree. |
| Is the gain durable? | Unknown. Novelty is plausible but untested. Varden's 24-month follow-up and a month-by-month analysis of the Halden data are the decisive next steps. |
| What drives the gain? | Unresolved. Rest and cutting low-value time like meetings are both candidates, and Varden's confirmatory test should help. |
| Coverage-bound work? | Output per employee and service fall, consistently across Halden retail, Halden reversions and the Varden counter stratum. Per-hour gains there likely reflect queueing, not productivity. |
| Sector-general? | No. What matters is whether output in a role depends on staff being present, as Varden argued. |

**What the comment would need to support its conclusion:**
1. Confidence intervals on every corrected estimate.
2. Every specification run on the same 17 organisations.
3. Bounds for the nine organisations that withdrew.
4. Results excluding billable-hours measures.
5. A month-by-month analysis of output per hour to test novelty directly.
6. Engagement with Varden's case-processing result.
